1:
That Paul calls it superfluous to write and then writes is read by almost everyone as deliberate. Chrysostom names the device: this is the rhetorical figure of omission, and it works because a hearer who sees what the speaker could have said and did not entertains no suspicion of him. He adds the motive, that a man given so high a character as to need no advice is ashamed to fall short of it. Robertson makes the point in a line, that the writing ought to be superfluous and all the same he does write. Ellicott insists there is no new subject here at all, the chapter division notwithstanding, only a continuation of the appeal to their self-respect begun a few verses earlier. Calvin faces the objection that Paul cannot mean it, since a man who thinks them prepared need not admonish and a man who doubts them should not call admonition unnecessary. His answer is that love carries both: good hope and anxious concern. He had seen a happy commencement and expected the progress to match it, but knowing the unsteadiness of the human mind could not guard too carefully. Henry reads the passage as skill, a man who seems to excuse his urging and by excusing it presses harder.

On why the brethren were sent ahead, Barnes puts most weight on what would have been lost if they had not been. Paul had boasted of Corinth to the Macedonians and moved them to give by it, so a failure now would touch his veracity and their character together, and he might be charged with trick in obtaining the Macedonian gift. Barnes quotes Bloomfield on the turn by which Paul says we, that we say not ye, should be ashamed, calling it inferior to none of the best classical writers; Robertson reads the same phrase as a delicate piece of syntax standing in for what Paul really means. Ellicott finds a further edge in the wording, that Macedonians appears without the article so as to rouse an esprit de corps: surely Achaians will not let Macedonians arrive and find them short of the account given. Clarke widens the field, noting that Achaia meant the whole Morea, so churches beyond Corinth were involved, Cenchrea among them. Gill raises the objection that sending anyone was needless if their forwardness was so well known, and answers it from the reason Paul gives. Henry notes the apology, that Paul did not want them surprised by hasty demands.

The word rendered bounty and the word set against it both get careful handling. Calvin takes the first from the Hebrew for blessing, which covers a prayer for another's prosperity as well as beneficence, and traces the double sense to its being ascribed first to God, whose blessing is effective by his simple will. Ellicott follows the same word forward instead of back, through its later use for the consecrated bread and wine, then the portions reserved for the sick and absent, then the unconsecrated remains, and at last gifts of bread to friends or the poor. Barnes keeps it practical, a gift fitted to confer happiness and to be a thank offering rather than something wrung out of them. On the opposite word Calvin observes that the Greek covers both excessive greed and mere niggardliness, the paring off of what ought to be given. Clarke locates the danger in how it would look: had they hung back, strangers would have imputed a covetous principle, as of men parting with money only when ashamed to keep it, whereas readiness to give is the mark of a liberal mind. Wesley puts it as bounty not wrung by importunity from covetous persons. Robertson observes that some offerings display covetousness by their very meanness, and that Paul, using the prefix a third time, rubs in that the pledge was overdue.
6:
Barnes hears a proverb in the sowing line, and works the figure out at length: money given away resembles seed committed to the earth, which may lie buried long enough that one ignorant of providence would suppose it lost, and yet springs up with ample increase. Calvin presses the same figure harder on its unpromising side, that the seed is scattered by hand, harrowed in, and rots, so that it seems as good as lost, and turns the comparison into an instrument: when carnal reason holds us back through fear of loss, this is the shield to lift, since God reckons what is laid out on the poor as lent to himself and repays it with large interest. Clarke supplies the background that makes the figure natural, that sowing was ordinary Jewish usage for almsgiving, and reads two prophetic passages as the rabbis did. Ellicott notes the same thought in the letter to the Galatians and draws the limit: what a man reaps answers not to the quantity of the gift, except as quantity indicates character, but to the spirit in which he gave it. Wesley states the rule in one line, that God proportions the reward to the work and to the temper it proceeds from. Robertson observes that the adverb for sparingly is late and rare.

On what it means to purpose in the heart the commentators divide sharply, and the division is practical. Henry makes deliberation a virtue and lists it among his three requirements: works of charity should be done with thought and design, whereas some do good only by accident, complying hastily with importunity, giving more than they intended and repenting of it, or giving less than full consideration would have prompted. Ellicott supports him from the verb, which appears nowhere else in the New Testament and carries its full ethical sense of a settled resolve deciding both the end and the means, not a passing impulse or a half-regretted promise. Barnes takes the opposite view and argues it at length. The heart is more concerned in giving than the head; the instinctive prompting of a benevolent heart is to give liberally; and a man who deliberates too long lets avarice in, begins comparing himself with others, and gives less than he first meant. His defence is that man at best is too selfish to be in much danger of giving too much. Gill stands apart from both by denying the verse is about amount at all, taking it to concern not any sum fixed in the mind but the manner of the giving.

Clarke explains the pair of negatives from the temple furniture. There were two chests for alms, one for what the law required and one for free-will offerings; of those who gave to the first nothing is said, of those who gave to the second much is said, and the apostle is evidently alluding to both. Calvin distinguishes two kinds of necessity to the same end. The necessity we impose on ourselves in obeying God is compatible with willingness, since we may constrain a reluctant flesh and act freely; what spoils the gift is constraint from the influence of others, which leaves a man wishing he could avoid the duty. Alms being a sacrifice, and no sacrifice pleasing unless voluntary, he concludes that God does not lord it over us as a tyrant but requires the cheerful obedience of children. Wesley catches the same thing in five words, of necessity being the state of a man who cannot tell how to refuse. Robertson notes that the word behind cheerful gives us hilarious, and that giving of necessity is like having eye-teeth pulled. Ellicott traces the whole clause to the Greek of Proverbs, where it differs markedly from the Hebrew, and takes it as evidence that Paul quoted habitually from that version.
8:
Calvin states the objection the verse is written against, in the voice of the man who feels it: what is given away is so much the less left for yourself. He answers that we are by nature excessively niggardly because we are prone to distrust, and that those who do good to the poor provide for themselves no less than a man watering his land, since almsgivings work like canals to make God's blessing flow back toward the giver. He is careful about the kind of power meant, adding that Paul speaks of it not as the poets do but as Scripture does, of a power put forth in action whose present efficacy is felt, not an inactive power we merely imagine. Barnes tests the promise against observation and reports that he can hardly point to anyone impoverished by liberality, our selfishness being a sufficient guard, while multitudes are made poor by the want of it, parsimonious in giving and extravagant in dress and amusement. Robertson notes that the verb for is able is a late one found almost nowhere but in Paul, and counts the threefold all of the verse. Wesley says each word is loaded with matter and increases all the way it goes.

Sufficiency is the word that draws the closest attention. Ellicott identifies it as a term of the Greek moralists, occurring only here and once in a later letter, and notes that self-sufficiency was for them the crown of the perfect life, vindicated by Aristotle for happiness and constantly on Stoic lips in Paul's own day. Robertson agrees the word shows an acquaintance with Stoicism, and adds the limit: Paul takes the ideal of independence from circumstances without taking the Cynic withdrawal from society that often went with it. Ellicott draws the practical line too, that what is promised is not the superfluity which ministers to selfish luxury but the competence disciples ought to be content with, and Calvin says the same by pointing out that the measure meant is the one God knows to be useful, since it is not always profitable for us to be filled to satiety. Calvin also finds a double provision in the promise, enough for themselves and something over for doing good. On the grace itself Clarke keeps to the sense the letter has been using, a charitable gift and so an abundance of temporal good, while Gill works by elimination through everything the phrase might mean before settling on the same thing.

The quotation from the psalm needs work to fit the argument, and three different repairs are offered. Clarke and Wesley take the word righteousness in the sense the Jews gave it, beneficence, so that what endures for ever is the good deed and its effects, Wesley adding that the store remains unexhausted because God keeps renewing it. Barnes reports that route as the common one and declines it, proposing instead that Paul cites part of a familiar passage while meaning the whole, since the psalm goes on to promise that the giver's horn shall be exalted with honour. Ellicott grants that the words might at first seem to describe God dispersing his own bounty rather than the almsgiver, and settles it from the parallelism of the psalm, where wealth in the house answers to righteousness enduring, so that the man can keep giving from a store continually replenished. On the verb itself Clarke keeps the sower in view, one who sows abroad among strangers and not only among those he knows, while Barnes suggests it may instead recall the eastern custom of scattering coin among a company of paupers. Robertson distinguishes the word for the poor here, a man who works for his living, from the word for an abject beggar.
10:
Whether these words are a promise or a prayer is a real question here, and Calvin makes it a textual one. Some manuscripts put the three verbs in the future, which would make the sentence a restatement of the promise just given, and Paul does repeat a promise in different words to impress it. Others give the infinitive, which can stand for an optative, and Calvin prefers that reading both as the more generally received and because Paul is accustomed to follow his exhortations with prayer for what he has just taught. Chrysostom had already made the same observation without the apparatus, noting that Paul states the thing not as an inference but in the form of a prayer, which makes his meaning plain and leads them on to hope from his praying and not only from what commonly happens. Barnes reads the clause the same way, as the expression of an earnest wish that they might experience in themselves what he had stated as a rule. Calvin adds what the circumlocution is for: sowing looks like the fountainhead from which food flows, and naming God as the one who supplies seed to the sower denies exactly that.

The verb behind supplieth draws the same discovery from two men who show no sign of consulting each other. Robertson traces it to the chorus-leader of the Greek stage and the practice of furnishing a chorus at one's own expense, which widened into supplying generally; Ellicott gives the same origin and adds a history, that the act was one of stately generosity, that the Greek Old Testament barely uses the word, that Paul appears to be the first to transfer it to the divine bounty, and that Peter takes it up later, perhaps having enriched his vocabulary from Paul's letters. Clarke arrives at the chorus independently again, and presses a different sense out of it, one who furnishes one thing after another so that there is no want or chasm, which he applies to providence connecting causes with effects. He also argues the point from creation: had God not made every plant with its seed in itself there would have been no seed to sow, and since the property is his gift he has the right to require how it be dispensed. Robertson settles a spelling on the way, preferring the form used in the Greek Bible of vegetable produce rather than the one used of animals.

Chrysostom describes the structure of the whole passage as deliberate alternation. Paul sets a spiritual return and a temporal one continually side by side, scattering abroad against multiplied seed, then back to the fruits of righteousness, and does it to give variety and to tear up their faint-hearted reasoning; and he draws the argument from the lesser: if God gives to those who sow the earth and feeds those who care for the body, much more to those who till the soil of heaven. On the enriching itself the others are unanimous that it is given for a use. Gill insists the promise is not merely sufficiency but an overplus, and that the overplus is for relieving the poor rather than for luxury. Clarke asks bluntly why God increases riches and answers that it is so all bountifulness may be exercised, warning that otherwise the rust will canker them. Barnes says property is given so it may be distributed in a way that causes thanksgiving, and adds that no one who truly loves his children wishes them rich for the sake of luxury. Calvin calls the contented mind the true affluence, since nothing is more starved than the distrustful. Wesley notes the thanksgiving rises from both sides, those who distribute and those who receive. Ellicott sees Paul already at Jerusalem, imagining the gifts announced.
12:
The word Paul chooses for this collection carries a history, and three of the commentators trace it. Robertson gives the derivation from the words for people and work, notes it covers public service whether rendered to God in worship or to others in benefaction, and observes that our word liturgy is this word. Ellicott follows it through three stages, from any public service to the State in classical Greek, to the ritual and sacrificial services of tabernacle and temple in the Greek Old Testament, to the ecclesiastical term applied at first only to the celebration of the Lord's Supper; and he draws the conclusion the history suggests, that a large gift to Christ's poor is the most acceptable of all forms of service in that liturgical sense. Calvin dwells on the classical end of it, the Athenian arrangement by which the richest citizens discharged burdensome public offices at their own expense in rotation. Barnes reports Doddridge's remark that the word marks this as an act of religion and not merely of humanity. Robertson adds a small thing the verb supplies, that it means to fill up by adding to, the Corinthians contributing their part to a total already gathered from others.

The proof or test in the next verse is read as an argument about evidence. Calvin says it was a sufficient token for bringing the love of the Corinthians to the trial that they were liberal to brethren at a great distance from them, and he extends it further, to their concurrence in obedience, which appears from alms being given with the common consent of all. Ellicott prefers the word test to experiment, and repairs the translation of what follows: not a professed subjection but an obedience to the confession of faith, the noun having acquired a half-technical sense like faith or religion used objectively. Robertson works the same noun from the other side, noting that it may mean either to profess, declaring openly, or to confess, saying the same thing as another, and that only context decides; and he states plainly what the collection was expected to prove, that the brethren in Jerusalem would learn from it that Gentiles make as good Christians as Jews. Barnes finds the older English of Tindale clearer than the received version here, and takes the doctrine to be that willingness to relieve the poor is one evidence that a profession is sincere. Wesley puts it in four words, subjection openly testified by actions.

The closing turn, that the relieved will pray for their benefactors, produces the strongest line in the chapter's commentary. Barnes argues that charity should be shown partly for this, since the prayers of the poorest Christian are worth more than what we usually bestow in charity, and a man who has secured the pleadings of a humble child of God has made good use of his money. He reads the intervening verse as a parenthesis, so that the service produces thanksgiving and also this. Calvin sees Paul refusing to omit any motive that might stir them: comfort, thanksgiving, a public confession of their unanimity, and now a return from the saints themselves, goodwill springing from gratitude and earnest prayer, so that the poor have the means of requiting the rich. Ellicott catches the mood rather than the argument, saying Paul seems half lost in anticipating the moment when the Gentile contributions are handed over at Jerusalem, and certain that praise will turn into intercession for the givers. Clarke lists the effects in order and then identifies the exceeding grace as the charitable disposition itself, which God furnished along with the means and the occasion. Gill takes the prayers to ask for blessings of the upper and the nether springs alike.
15:
What the unspeakable gift is turns out to be genuinely contested, and Barnes and Clarke take opposite sides of the same earlier proposal. Barnes reports the suggestion that it means the charitable disposition the Corinthians had shown, and dismisses it as falling far below the design of the passage. For him the reference is to the Son given to die for them, and he makes the abruptness itself the evidence: it is a striking instance of a mind so full of that subject that wherever Paul began he was sure to end at the Redeemer, the gift so familiar to his private thoughts that the remotest allusion turned him toward it. Clarke argues the other way and by close reading rather than sentiment. The unspeakable gift, he says, is precisely the same thing as the superabounding grace named in the previous verse; that grace was plainly the work of Christ in them and not Christ himself; therefore what is praised here is the work and not the operator. He grants freely that the Son is an unspeakable blessing which angels desire to look into, and denies only that it is what this verse means.

Between those two positions the others decline to choose, and one of them says so outright. Ellicott lists the candidates and the evidence for each, that the usage in Acts favours the gift of the Spirit while the usage in Romans favours the gift of pardon or righteousness, and then sets the whole question aside on a point of temperament: it probably never entered Paul's thoughts to subject a jubilant utterance of praise to minute analysis. Gill offers three readings in succession without ranking them, the goodness of God shown to giver and receiver alike, the exceeding grace bestowed in their effectual calling, or Christ himself, whom he grants at once to be beyond question an unspeakable gift, since none can tell how great it is or declare the love of Father and Son expressed in it. Wesley takes the widest reading available, the outward and inward blessings together, whose number and excellence cannot be uttered, which leaves the question of reference open by including everything that could answer to it.

On how the sentence behaves, rather than what it denotes, two observations stand out. Robertson counts this as the third time in five verses that Paul has given thanks to God, and describes the line as one of his gems flashed out after a tangled passage like a gleam of light clearing the air; he suspects the adjective was coined for the occasion, since it appears nowhere else outside later church writers except as a variant reading in one Hellenistic text, where it describes a wonder beyond description, and he sets it beside the unsearchable of the doxology in Romans. Ellicott reads the same abruptness as a fact about the dictation. There was manifestly a pause here, longer or shorter, in which fresh thoughts of another kind were working and rousing very different feelings, before Paul broke silence and began again on a new subject. Read that way the verse is not a summary of what precedes but the last thing said before an interval, which suits both the compression Robertson notices and the difficulty the others have in fixing its reference.
